Everything here is my own work. Where I used environment, character or weapon assets from the Unity Asset Store, Sketchfab or Hero Forge, I’ve said so in the caption.

Games

Zombie Survival FPS

Unity · Blender · C#

A first-person survival horror game set after a zombie outbreak — survival, horror, apocalypse. My final and largest project, and the only one where the level existed as technical drawings before it existed in the engine.

What I built

  • Drew a ground plan and scaled wall elevations for an L-shaped garden level
  • Modelled it in Blender — extruded the floor plan into walls, applied materials, set up lighting for atmosphere
  • Chose the L-shape deliberately: the player can’t see round the corner, which builds tension
  • Blocked out the environment in Unity and set the player controller up as a prefab
  • Built a weapon with three fire modes and destructible objects to shoot at
  • Wrote the design documentation — concept, MDA framework, protagonist motivation and backstory

Scripts I wrote

  • FPSController — movement, mouse look, and gravity so movement feels weighted rather than floaty
  • Weapon — single, burst and automatic fire modes, with bullet spread calculated from the camera’s forward vector
  • Bullet — collision detection that tags targets, walls and bottles separately, spawns an impact decal, and shatters bottles when they’re hit

Main Menu & Interface

Unity UI

Designed on paper first, then built in Unity with working buttons and hover states. This is the piece of the work that connects directly to the UI and UX research in my written portfolio.

Spaceship Canyon Shooter

Unity · Terrain Tools · C#

Fly a ship through a canyon, firing lasers and staying inside the boundaries. The first project where I designed on paper before touching the engine.

What I built

  • Drew the ship by hand first — thrusters, cockpit, power, main systems, and an arrowhead nose for aerodynamics
  • Modelled and lit that design in Unity
  • Sculpted the canyon with Unity Terrain Tools, then painted it with layered rock, grass and sand textures
  • Used post-processing to get the lighting and atmosphere right

Scripts I wrote

  • ShipController — movement, rotation and laser fire, clamping the ship inside the play area
  • PlayerControls — flight on all axes, pitch/yaw/roll driven by input, and laser particle systems toggled on fire

Obstacle Course Platformer

Unity · C#

A jumping course where the player crosses platforms and spinning obstacles to reach the finish. My first 3D Unity build, and where I learned to write and debug C# properly.

What I built

  • Designed the level layout, then built the map in Unity
  • Added colours and materials to make the route readable to the player
  • Tested each obstacle in play mode and fixed what broke

Scripts I wrote

  • Spinner — rotates an obstacle continuously from X, Y and Z values exposed in the Inspector
  • PlayerMoveJumpHit3D — movement and jumping, turning objects yellow on collision while excluding the ground
  • Restart — reloads the active scene through SceneManager when the player hits a trigger

2D Delivery Taxi

Unity · C#

A top-down driving game where you deliver packages to houses around a city. My first Unity project, built the year before the 3D ones.

What I built

  • Built the city from scratch — road network, junctions, roundabouts, buildings and greenery
  • Set up colliders so the car stays on the road and the buildings block it
  • Added the delivery logic: pick up a package, drive it to the right house, drop it off
  • Tuned the camera to follow the car as it drives

What I learned

  • How a Unity scene is actually assembled, layer by layer, from an empty project
  • That level design is mostly iteration — the map was rebuilt several times before it drove well
  • How sprites, colliders and scripts fit together, which made the 3D projects far less daunting

3D & Character Work

Blender — Modelling & Lighting

Blender

Learning Blender properly: modelling from scratch, materials, lighting and rendering. The donuts were practice I did at home in my own time; the room was a college brief to recreate a real interior from a photograph.

Character Design & Sprite Sheets

Hero Forge · Blender · Photopea

Designing a cast of characters, taking one of them into Blender as a 3D model, and cutting animation frames into sprite sheets ready for a 2D game.

What I did

  • Designed eight characters in Hero Forge — silhouette, pose, equipment and colour scheme chosen to make each one readable at a glance
  • Wrote a short backstory and colour rationale for each, using colour symbolism to signal role and personality
  • Exported one character and rebuilt it in Blender to learn the import and modelling workflow
  • Rendered fighting, running and dying animation frames and assembled them into sprite sheets in Photopea

Note on tools

  • Hero Forge is a character creator — the base meshes are theirs. The design decisions, posing, equipment, colour schemes and backstories are mine.
  • The Blender model and the sprite sheet assembly are my own work.

Written Work

Research & Analysis

Written portfolio

Roughly half the course was written research, graded at Distinction for Informing Ideas and Communication.

  • Accessibility and inclusive design — the barriers players with visual, hearing, mobility and cognitive impairments face, and the features modern games use to remove them
  • UI and UX evaluation — comparing what works and what doesn’t across released commercial games
  • Player motivation — Maslow’s hierarchy of needs applied to how games hold attention
  • Conditioning and reward design — Pavlov and Skinner, and how reward loops shape play
  • Game addiction — what turns a hobby into a problem, and how design decisions contribute
  • Design documentation — concept, MDA framework, character motivation, ground plans and scaled elevations

All code, level design, 3D modelling, character design and written work here is my own. Environment, character and weapon assets were sourced from the Unity Asset Store, Sketchfab and Hero Forge and remain the property of their creators.
